tldr: Humanoid motion-tracking training used to require GPU clusters costing tens of millions of yen. By introducing a differentiable world model that captures shared physical dynamics, this paper compresses training to a single GPU in just 3 hours and demonstrates transfer to a physical robot.
hero_caption: Overview of policy optimization using imagined rollouts inside a learned differentiable world model. While prior work (SONIC) required 128 GPUs running for 7 days (about 21,000 GPU-hours), SuperMimic surpasses it on a single H100 GPU in just 3 hours, slashing compute by more than 1000x.
overview:
To give humanoid robots human-like, agile, and expressive movements, tracking large-scale motion capture (mocap) datasets via reinforcement learning has become the dominant approach. However, scaling across more motions causes training costs to explode. The prior state-of-the-art model, SONIC, required running 128 GPUs for a full week. Why was so much compute needed? Existing methods rely on model-free reinforcement learning (such as PPO). Regardless of how diverse the motions are, they ignore the shared physical dynamics—the fact that the robot's physical body is identical across all motions—and repeat noisy simulation trials from scratch.

The authors asked: since body dynamics are shared, can we train a single differentiable world model (a neural surrogate simulator) that mimics the rigid-body simulator, and update the policy via backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) with analytic gradients to drastically boost efficiency?

Testing this idea showed that SuperMimic surpassed SONIC's tracking performance on a single GPU in just 3 hours. That is a compute reduction of over 1000x in GPU-hours. Furthermore, on a massive benchmark of 129,514 motions where prior work fell and failed on 179 clips, SuperMimic achieved zero failures (a 100% success rate) after only 9.8 hours of training on two GPUs. The learned controller transferred directly to a physical Unitree G1 without tuning, successfully performing highly dynamic acrobatic movements such as cartwheels and flips. This work removes the massive compute bottleneck, lowering humanoid whole-body control scaling down to a single GPU in any research lab.
contributions: Successfully demonstrated, for the first time, Sim-to-Real transfer of a humanoid whole-body controller trained with model-based RL (a differentiable world model + BPTT), in a domain previously dominated by model-free PPO.
Surpassed the state-of-the-art cluster-scale method (SONIC, trained on 128 GPUs for 7 days) in just 3 hours on a single GPU, reducing GPU-hours by more than 1000x.

Analyzed the key drivers of computational efficiency, showing stable world model prediction errors even with a 264x increase in motion data, rollouts 10x to 60x faster than the simulator, and dramatic sample efficiency from analytic gradients.
Enabled a flexible interface learning framework using the same world model to train policies directly with downstream task-specific rewards (such as velocity command tracking) via RL.

sections.heading: Why Did Humanoid Whole-Body Control Require Massive GPU Clusters?
sections.summary: Physics-based imitation of large mocap datasets is the standard path for humanoid control, but compute costs have exploded as motion diversity expanded. This paper breaks the compute bottleneck by unifying the robot's shared dynamical system into a single differentiable world model that provides analytic gradients.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to operate in human-centered environments, they need whole-body controllers covering a wide range of movements, from walking and running to dancing, crouching, and recovering from falls. Recent approaches extract motion clips from large motion capture datasets and train tracking policies using reinforcement learning.

However, expanding motion coverage hits an enormous computational wall. For instance, SONIC, a recent state-of-the-art method, required approximately 168 hours of training on 128 GPUs (around 21,000 GPU-hours). This heavy cost stems from either distilling separate specialist models or brute-forcing a monolithic policy using model-free RL (PPO) across thousands of parallel simulation environments.

A key fact often overlooked is that no matter how diverse the target motions are, the humanoid's hybrid rigid-body dynamics—its morphology and contact physics—remain exactly the same. Model-free RL ignores this shared structure and repeatedly estimates action consequences from scratch using noisy simulation rollouts. In short, scaling motions directly triggered an explosion in compute.

SuperMimic eliminates this inefficiency by introducing a single differentiable world model fitted from logged simulator transitions. By performing backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) over short imagined rollouts, it directly provides the policy with accurate, low-variance analytic gradients. Because it differentiates through a neural surrogate model rather than the rigid-body simulator itself, it maintains full compatibility with non-differentiable physics engines and discontinuous contact events.

sections.heading: Challenging Model-Free Dominance with Differentiable Model-Based RL
sections.summary: This section frames how SuperMimic distinguishes itself across four areas: physics-based motion tracking, differentiable simulation, model-based RL for robotics, and downstream interface design.
sections.details:
### Large-Scale Physics-Based Motion Tracking
From DeepMimic and PHC to SONIC, mocap tracking has become the standard recipe for broad humanoid behavioral repertoires. Yet, all these successes rely on massive simulation rollouts, making compute consumption the primary scaling bottleneck.

### Learned Differentiable Dynamics for Motion Control
Training neural surrogates of simulators to optimize control policies via analytic gradients has been explored in computer animation, such as in SuperTrack, ControlVAE, and SuperDyno. SuperMimic scales this paradigm to large-scale humanoid tracking on a single GPU and brings it to physical hardware (Sim-to-Real). For hardware transfer, it employs an asymmetric observation design: the world model receives simulation context (domain randomization parameters), while the policy only observes noisy proprioception.

### Model-Based Policy Optimization and Robot Deployment
Model-based RL (MBRL) methods like the Dreamer family, DayDreamer, and TD-MPC have shown strong performance by imagining in latent spaces. Short-horizon actor-critics like SHAC also leverage differentiable simulators. Recent frameworks like RWM and RWM-U train policies on learned neural simulators and deploy them to real robots; however, they pretrain the world model on data from external policies and use PPO for policy optimization. In contrast, SuperMimic keeps the world model updated online with on-policy data and optimizes the policy directly via BPTT with analytic gradients instead of PPO.

### Reuse for Downstream Task Control
When connecting learned motor skills to downstream tasks like velocity command or end-effector tracking, prior work mostly relied on motion distillation. SuperMimic shows that the same world model can be reused to optimize goal encoders directly via RL using task-specific reward functions.

captions.P3: Comparison of training strategies between prior work and SuperMimic. SuperMimic unifies motion tracking (Mimic) and latent representations (Latent) within a single MBRL loop. Downstream tasks can be optimized via task-specific RL rather than pure distillation, and real-robot deployment is demonstrated.

sections.heading: Learning by Imagining: Architecture and Training Loop of SuperMimic
sections.summary: SuperMimic executes three phases—data collection, world model fitting, and policy optimization via the world model—in a single unified loop. Flowing analytic gradients through short imagined rollouts while bootstrapping long-term value with a critic yields stable, highly efficient policy updates.
sections.details:
### 3.1 The Overall SuperMimic Training Loop
Training alternates through three phases inside a single loop:
- **(1) Data Collection**: The current policy $\pi_\theta$ executes in the simulator with added action noise, storing transition data into a fixed-size replay buffer $\mathcal{B}$.
- **(2) World Model Fitting**: Subsequences of $k$ steps ($k=8$ in this work) are sampled from the buffer to train the differentiable world model $f_\omega$ autoregressively via supervised learning.
- **(3) Policy Improvement via World Model**: With the world model frozen, the policy generates imagined rollouts of horizon $H=32$ starting from buffer states. Policy $\pi_\theta$ and critic $V_\psi$ are updated simultaneously using backpropagation-through-time (BPTT).

Because the underlying physical laws of the body do not change, transitions collected by older policies remain fully valid for training the world model.

### 3.2 Fitting the Differentiable World Model
The model serves as a neural surrogate for the rigid-body simulator. Domain randomization parameters—such as friction coefficients, link centers of mass, and calibration offsets—are fed into the model as a simulation context $\xi$, allowing it to treat stochastic environment variations deterministically. The model predicts the next state $\hat{s}_{t+1} = f_\omega(\hat{s}_t, a_t, \xi)$, clean observations $\bar{o}_t$, rewards $\hat{r}_{t+1}$, and differentiable episode termination probabilities $\hat{d}_t \in [0, 1]$. Training on an autoregressive window of $k=8$ steps teaches the model to self-correct compound prediction errors.

### 3.3 Policy Optimization via the World Model
During policy updates, imagined rollouts run for $H=32$ steps from states sampled from the buffer. Known sensor noise $\eta_t$ is deliberately injected into the clean observation $\bar{o}_t$ produced by the model before feeding it to the policy ($a_t = \pi_\theta(\bar{o}_t + \eta_t, g_t)$).

The policy objective $\hat{J}(\theta)$ is defined as the sum of cumulative rewards over the rollout and the terminal state value estimated by the critic $V_\psi$ at step $H$. By backpropagating returns through the differentiable dynamics directly to actions and policy parameters via BPTT, gradient variance is dramatically lower than in black-box score-function methods like PPO.

Adopting an actor-critic structure inspired by SHAC, the policy bootstraps future returns beyond horizon $H$ via a critic trained with Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE). This enables farsighted decision-making while keeping the rollout horizon short ($H=32$ steps = 0.64 seconds), right where model predictions are most accurate.

sections.heading: Empirical Proof: 1000x Less Compute, 129k Motions Completed, and Real-Robot Deployment
sections.summary: On a 129k-motion benchmark, SuperMimic outperformed SONIC (128 GPUs, 7 days) in 3 hours on 1 GPU, and achieved zero failures in 9.8 hours on 2 GPUs. Ablations quantified the gains from fast rollouts and analytic gradients, and acrobatic transfer was verified on a Unitree G1.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Outperforming SONIC with Drastically Reduced Compute
Experiments were conducted using MuJoCo Warp, a GPU-native physics engine. On a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, SuperMimic surpassed the normalized return of SONIC's public checkpoint (trained on 128 L40 GPUs for 7 days, or ~21,000 GPU-hours) in only 3 hours. That represents an over 1000x reduction in GPU-hours.

Across the full BONES-SEED benchmark of 129,514 motions, SONIC failed (fell) on 179 clips. SuperMimic reduced failures to 25 after 3 hours on 1 GPU, and achieved zero failures (a 100% completion rate) when trained for 9.8 hours on 2 GPUs. In comparison against a direct simulator baseline running PPO (PPO-Sim) on the LAFAN1 dataset, PPO-Sim failed to reach the target return (0.82) even after 18 hours across 8 GPUs, whereas SuperMimic easily reached it on 1 GPU in 1.2 hours.

### 4.2 Three Key Drivers of Compute Reduction
The authors dissected why SuperMimic achieves such speed:
- **Robustness to Motion Volume**: Scaling the dataset length 264-fold (from 1 to 264 hours) kept the world model's 8-step prediction error stable between 0.007 and 0.011. Since body physics remain identical regardless of motion quantity, the model capacity does not saturate.
- **Blazing Fast Rollouts**: World model inference was over 10x faster than MuJoCo Warp simulations across 2k to 16k parallel environments, and up to 62x faster at 64k environments.
- **Sample Efficiency of Analytic Gradients**: Comparing against PPO run on the world model (PPO-WM), SuperMimic's BPTT policy updates required approximately 1/64th the imagined steps to match PPO-WM's peak return. The speedup stems not just from faster rollouts, but from the superior quality of analytic gradients.

### 4.3 Critic Necessity and Disturbance Recovery
Ablating horizon $H$ revealed that training collapsed when $H \le 16$ without a critic. In push-recovery tests applying 0.5 to 4 m/s external impulses during a stance pose, the critic-enabled policy recovered posture within 0.5 to 2.4 seconds. In contrast, the critic-free policy stumbled erratically and fell at 4 m/s. This proves the critic accurately accounts for recovery beyond the short imagined horizon.

### 4.4 Sim-to-Real Transfer on a Physical Humanoid
The tracking controller was deployed directly onto a physical Unitree G1 robot without per-motion tuning. It successfully executed dynamic locomotion like skipping, ground-contact maneuvers like side rolls where the torso and limbs touch the floor, and acrobatic moves including 90-degree and stationary 360-degree flips.

### 4.5 Downstream Task Control: RL Encoder vs. Distillation Baseline
Sharing the same world model, a velocity command encoder was trained directly via RL using a velocity-tracking reward. Compared to distillation baselines that match reference motion latents, the RL-trained encoder achieved smaller steady-state errors in 650 out of 672 velocity step-response tests and remained completely stable even during sharp turning commands.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Democratizing Humanoid Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: By amortizing learning across entire motion datasets using a single shared differentiable world model, SuperMimic removes compute as the primary bottleneck in humanoid whole-body control. Tracking scaling laws can now be measured on a single GPU.
sections.details:
The core achievement of this work is demonstrating that large-scale humanoid whole-body control, previously deemed impossible without cluster-scale GPU infrastructure, can be trained on a single workstation GPU in an ordinary lab.

Pairing a differentiable world model that captures shared body dynamics with short-horizon backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) slashes training time by orders of magnitude, eliminates tracking failures, and achieves zero-shot transfer to a physical Unitree G1. Moving forward, researchers can explore motion tracking scaling laws on individual GPUs without worrying about prohibitive cloud compute bills.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Directions
sections.summary: The authors highlight key limitations and future directions, including simultaneous multi-interface learning, dynamics adaptation from real-world data, and handling uneven terrain and object manipulation.
sections.details:
The paper outlines several clear limitations and avenues for future work:
- **Incomplete Validation of Multi-Interface Learning**: In this paper's experiments, the velocity encoder was trained concurrently with motion tracking, but gradients from the velocity reward were stopped before updating the shared decoder. This makes it practically equivalent to post-hoc encoder training, leaving the effects of fully joint optimization of the shared decoder unexplored.
- **Simulator-Dependent Dynamics**: The world model is currently trained exclusively on logged transitions from a rigid-body simulator. Future extensions could fine-tune the world model using real-robot run logs or use its differentiability for high-precision system identification (parameter estimation).
- **Flat-Terrain Restriction**: SuperMimic was trained only on flat ground. Extending the framework to rough terrain with steps or obstacles, as well as interactions with external objects like furniture and parcels, remains an important next step.

takeaways: Leveraging the insight that physical body dynamics remain identical regardless of motion diversity makes amortizing physics into a single shared differentiable world model extremely effective.
Replacing model-free PPO with short-horizon analytic gradients (BPTT) through a learned surrogate model bootstrapped by a critic reduces compute requirements by over 1000x.
Increasing motion data hundreds of times does not degrade world model prediction accuracy; adding motions strengthens model generalization and robustness.
Whole-body control policies learned in this framework are not confined to simulation; they transfer directly to physical humanoids, even for dynamic and acrobatic movements, without manual tuning.
limitations: Restricted to flat ground; does not yet support uneven terrain, stairs, obstacles, or contact and manipulation with external objects.
The world model relies entirely on rigid-body simulator data and does not directly incorporate real-robot non-linearities or joint backlash during world model training.
During downstream task training (such as velocity control), gradient updates to the shared decoder are blocked, leaving true joint multi-task optimization still in the validation stage.
